PETITION TO DETERMINE SUCCESSION TO REAL PROPERTY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · March 15, 2026

PETITION TO DETERMINE SUCCESSION TO REAL PROPERTY — INFORMATION AND BACKGROUND
This information sheet discusses the California superior court petition procedure of Probate Code §§ 13150-13157, a court order determining succession to real property, in connection with the estate of Pat Morgan, who died on March 15, 2026. Jordan Morgan is a successor of Pat Morgan with respect to real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, California, described as Lot 4, Block 2, Tract No. 1234, as per map recorded in Book 10, Page 5 of Maps, Sacramento County and identified by Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, with a gross value stated as $620,000. Under this procedure, a petition may be filed in the superior court for Sacramento County, California, requesting a court order determining that the described real property, which was Pat Morgan's primary residence, has passed to Jordan Morgan as a successor of Pat Morgan. This document is background information only. It is not the petition itself, is not filed with any court, and does not by itself request, obtain, or constitute any court order. Only a petition actually filed with the superior court, followed by the statutory notice, and a hearing resulting in a signed court order, can determine that the described real property has passed to Jordan Morgan.

WHEN THIS COURT-ORDER PROCEDURE IS AVAILABLE
California Probate Code § 13150 limits use of the court-order-determining-succession procedure of Chapter 4 (§§ 13150-13157) to one of two situations: no proceeding for administration of the decedent's estate is being or has been conducted in California, or the decedent's personal representative has consented in writing to use of this procedure specifically to determine that real property that was the decedent's primary residence passes to the petitioners. As currently written, the chapter's own text ties this procedure to the decedent's "primary residence" specifically, and § 13150(b)(2) clarifies that for this chapter, "primary residence" is not limited to the residence the decedent occupied at the time of death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "13150. The procedure provided by this chapter may be used only if one of the following requirements is satisfied: (a) No proceeding is being or has been conducted in this state for administration of the decedent’s estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13150(a), California Probate Code, first condition for using this procedure — no estate proceeding pending (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13150.)
  "(b) (1) The decedent’s personal representative consents in writing to use of the procedure provided by this chapter to determine that real property that was the decedent’s primary residence is property passing to the petitioners. (2) For purposes of this chapter, “primary residence” is not limited to the decedent’s residence at the time of their death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13150(b), California Probate Code, second condition — personal representative's written consent, and the chapter's definition of "primary residence" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13150.)

The current text was amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 331 (AB 2016), effective January 1, 2025, and its own "primary residence" limitation is new to that amendment; this document did not fetch or independently verify the section's pre-January 1, 2025 text, and does not describe what this chapter covered, or how it differed, before that date — only what the current, in-force text provides. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific proceeding is or is not pending for a specific decedent's estate, or that a described property was in fact a specific decedent's primary residence.

WHO MAY FILE, THE DOLLAR THRESHOLD, AND THE 40-DAY WAIT
California Probate Code § 13151(a) lets "the successor of the decedent to an interest in" the decedent's primary-residence real property file this petition, without first procuring letters of administration or awaiting probate of the will, once two conditions are met: the real property's gross value does not exceed a statutory dollar ceiling (currently $750,000, adjusted periodically under § 890), and at least 40 days have elapsed since the decedent's death. The petition is filed "in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the decedent may be administered," and it requests a court order determining that the petitioner has succeeded to the described real property.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) If a decedent dies leaving real property that was their primary residence in this state and the gross value of that real property does not exceed seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890, and 40 days have elapsed since the death of the decedent, the successor of the decedent to an interest in that real property, without procuring letters of administration or awaiting the probate of the will, may file a petition in the superior court of the county in which the estate of the decedent may be administered requesting a court order determining that the petitioner has succeeded to that real property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13151(a), California Probate Code, who may file, the dollar threshold, and the 40-day wait (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13151.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of who may file this specific petition and under what dollar and timing conditions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that any specific petitioner in fact qualifies as a "successor" under this section for any specific decedent's property. The $750,000 figure quoted in § 13151(a)'s own text is the amount that currently applies only because of the specific decedent's-death date window described in a companion clause of this document (Probate Code § 13152(f)); this document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 890 or the Judicial Council's own published schedule of periodically adjusted dollar amounts. This clause cites a single statutory subdivision (§ 13151(a)); § 13151(b), addressing a separate notice obligation, is covered in a companion clause. This document is informational only; it does not itself determine that any specific petitioner qualifies to file, or that any specific property in fact does not exceed the applicable dollar ceiling.

THE DOLLAR THRESHOLD HAS CHANGED SUBSTANTIALLY, ON A STATUTORY SCHEDULE
The dollar ceiling that governs this procedure is not a single fixed number; California Probate Code § 13152(f) writes a four-part schedule directly into the statute's own text. For a decedent who died before April 1, 2022, the applicable amount is $166,250. For a death on or after April 1, 2022 through March 31, 2025, the applicable amount is "the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent's death" — a figure this section does not itself restate. For a death on or after April 1, 2025 through March 31, 2028, the statute states a new flat figure directly: $750,000. For a death on or after April 1, 2028, the applicable amount reverts to whatever adjusted figure is then published under § 890. This entire schedule, including the current $750,000 figure, was written into § 13152 by Stats. 2024, Ch. 331 (AB 2016), effective January 1, 2025.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(f) (1) If the decedent dies prior to April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250). (2) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2022, through March 31, 2025, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent’s death. (3) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2028, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000). (4) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2028, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13152(f), California Probate Code, the four-part dollar-threshold schedule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13152.)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 331, Sec. 5. (AB 2016) Effective January 1, 2025.)"
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13152 enactment note, California Probate Code, amendment history confirming the January 1, 2025 effective date (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13152.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific dollar-threshold schedule California law currently applies to this procedure — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or about which of the four listed figures applies to any decedent whose date of death this document does not itself state elsewhere. This document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 890 itself or the Judicial Council's own published table of periodically adjusted dollar amounts, so the specific figure that applied between April 1, 2022 and March 31, 2025, or that will apply on or after April 1, 2028, is not stated here beyond the statute's own cross-reference. Separately, this document did not fetch or verify the pre-January 1, 2025 text of § 13152 itself, so it does not describe what dollar figure or scope applied under the prior version of this section, only that the current, in-force schedule was enacted by the cited 2024 amendment. The quoted schedule (four paragraphs of subdivision (f)) and the quoted enactment note are both drawn from the same statutory section and are treated as one source, not independent ones.

REQUIRED CONTENTS OF THE PETITION, AND THE PROBATE-REFEREE APPRAISAL
California Probate Code § 13152(a) requires the petition to be verified by each petitioner and to state, among other things, facts establishing proper venue and that the real property's gross value (as shown by an attached inventory and appraisal) does not exceed the applicable dollar ceiling. Among the petition's other required contents, § 13152(a)(7) requires disclosure of "the name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent," the names and addresses of anyone named as an executor of the decedent's will, and, where the petitioner is trustee of a trust that is itself a devisee under the will, the names and addresses of persons interested in that trust. Separately, § 13152(b) requires an inventory and appraisal, in the form set out in Probate Code § 8802, to be attached to the petition, with the appraisal made by a probate referee the petitioner selects from those the Controller has appointed under § 400 for the county where the property is located.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) The petition shall be verified by each petitioner, shall contain a request that the court make an order under this chapter determining that the property described in the petition is property passing to the petitioner, and shall state all of the following: (1) The facts necessary to determine that the petition is filed in the proper county. (2) The gross value of the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence in this state, as shown by the inventory and appraisal attached to the petition, does not exceed the dollar amount specified in subdivision (f)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13152(a) intro, (1)-(2), California Probate Code, verification requirement and first two required contents (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13152.)
  "(7) The name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent, the names and addresses of all persons named as executors of the will of the decedent, and, if the petitioner is the trustee of a trust that is a devisee under the will of the decedent, the names and addresses of all persons interested in the trust, as determined in cases of future interests pursuant to paragraph (1), (2), or (3) of subdivision (a) of Section 15804, so far as known to any petitioner."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13152(a)(7), California Probate Code, required disclosure of heirs, devisees, and named executors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13152.)
  "(b) An inventory and appraisal in the form set forth in Section 8802 of the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence in this state shall be attached to the petition. The appraisal shall be made by a probate referee selected by the petitioner from those probate referees appointed by the Controller under Section 400 to appraise property in the county where the real property is located. The appraisal shall be made as provided in Part 3 (commencing with Section 8800) of Division 7."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13152(b), California Probate Code, required inventory and appraisal by a probate referee (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13152.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of what a petition under this chapter must state and attach — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that any particular petition satisfies these requirements. This clause quotes § 13152(a)'s introductory language together with paragraphs (1) and (2), and separately quotes paragraph (7) and subdivision (b) verbatim; it does not quote paragraphs (3) through (6) or (8) verbatim (covering, among other things, the property description, the basis for the petitioner's claim, disclosure of any other-jurisdiction proceedings, and disclosure of any guardian or conservator of the decedent's estate) — those additional required items exist in the statute's text but are not independently quoted here. § 13152(a) and § 13152(b) are subdivisions of one statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent ones. This document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 8802 (the referenced inventory-and-appraisal form) or § 400 (probate referee appointment) themselves. This document is informational only; it does not itself verify, attach, or complete any petition, inventory, or appraisal.

TWO SEPARATE NOTICE REQUIREMENTS: TO NAMED HEIRS AND DEVISEES, AND OF THE HEARING
This procedure carries two separate statutory notice obligations. First, California Probate Code § 13151(b) requires a successor who files this petition to "deliver a notice of the petition to each heir and devisee named in the petition pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 13152" within five business days of filing. Second, and separately, Probate Code § 13153 requires that "[n]otice of the hearing shall be given as provided in Section 1220 to each of the persons named in the petition pursuant to Section 13152" — a broader notice obligation than § 13151(b)'s, since it reaches every person § 13152 requires the petition to name (heirs, devisees, named executors, trust beneficiaries where relevant, and any guardian or conservator of the decedent's estate), not only heirs and devisees.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(b) A successor who files a petition pursuant to subdivision (a) shall deliver a notice of the petition to each heir and devisee named in the petition pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 13152 within five business days of filing the petition."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13151(b), California Probate Code, five-business-day notice to named heirs and devisees (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13151.)
  "13153. Notice of the hearing shall be given as provided in Section 1220 to each of the persons named in the petition pursuant to Section 13152."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13153, California Probate Code, notice of the hearing under Section 1220 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13153.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of two distinct notice obligations this procedure imposes — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, or that notice given in any specific case satisfied either requirement. § 13151(b) and § 13153 are two separately numbered, independently verified statutory sections. This document did not independently fetch or verify Probate Code § 1220, the general notice-of-hearing procedure § 13153 cross-references, so the specific mechanics of how that hearing notice must be given (method, timing before the hearing, and to whom beyond those named under § 13152) are not described here. This document is informational only; it does not itself deliver, serve, or determine the adequacy of notice to any specific heir, devisee, or other interested person.

WHAT THE COURT MUST DETERMINE BEFORE ISSUING THE ORDER
California Probate Code § 13154(a) provides that if the court makes the determinations required under subdivision (b), the court "shall issue an order determining that the real property that was the decedent's primary residence...is property passing to the petitioners and the specific property interest of each petitioner in the described property." Subdivision (b)'s required determinations include the property's gross value, the 40-day wait, the applicable no-proceeding-or-consent condition, and that the described property is in fact property of the decedent passing to the petitioner. Section 13154(c) then supplies an evidentiary shortcut on the value determination specifically: where the petition has an inventory and appraisal attached that satisfies § 13152(b), the court makes the gross-value determination "on the basis of the verified petition and the attached inventory and appraisal," unless a person opposing the petition offers evidence that the property's gross value actually exceeds the applicable dollar ceiling.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) If the court makes the determinations required under subdivision (b), the court shall issue an order determining that the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence, to be described in the order, is property passing to the petitioners and the specific property interest of each petitioner in the described property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13154(a), California Probate Code, the order the court must issue once it makes the required determinations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13154.)
  "(c) If the petition has attached an inventory and appraisal that satisfies the requirements of subdivision (b) of Section 13152, the determination required by paragraph (1) of subdivision (b) of this section shall be made on the basis of the verified petition and the attached inventory and appraisal, unless evidence is offered by a person opposing the petition that the gross value of the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence in this state exceeds seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000), as adjusted periodically in accordance with Section 890."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13154(c), California Probate Code, evidentiary effect of an attached inventory and appraisal on the value determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13154.)

This clause quotes § 13154(a) and § 13154(c) verbatim; § 13154(b)'s four numbered determinations are described in this clause's body in paraphrase rather than quoted verbatim, and a reader should treat that paraphrase, not an independently verified quotation, as this document's account of subdivision (b)'s specific wording. § 13154(a) and § 13154(c) are subdivisions of the same statutory section and are treated here as one source, not independent ones. This document is informational only; it does not itself make any of these determinations or issue any order.

THE ORDER'S FINALITY: CONCLUSIVE ON ALL PERSONS, WHETHER OR NOT YET IN BEING
California Probate Code § 13155 gives a final order under this chapter unusually broad, self-contained finality: "Upon becoming final, an order under this chapter determining that property is property passing to the petitioner is conclusive on all persons, whether or not they are in being." The statute's own wording extends this conclusiveness to persons not yet in existence at the time of the order — for example, a not-yet-born future heir or beneficiary — not only to the parties and persons actually given notice of the petition.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Upon becoming final, an order under this chapter determining that property is property passing to the petitioner is conclusive on all persons, whether or not they are in being."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13155, California Probate Code, finality and conclusiveness of the order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13155.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the specific finality effect California law gives this particular kind of order — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific order, or about when any specific order actually "becomes final" for purposes of this section. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 13155); no additional independent source was found for it, and this document did not independently fetch or verify the general California appellate-finality rules (for example, the time to appeal a probate order) that determine when an order "becomes final" in the first place — this section's text does not itself define that term. THE PETITIONER'S PERSONAL LIABILITY FOR THE DECEDENT'S UNSECURED DEBTS
Receiving property under this chapter carries a liability consequence. California Probate Code § 13156(a) provides that, subject to subdivisions (b) through (d), "the petitioner who receives the decedent's property pursuant to an order under this chapter is personally liable for the unsecured debts of the decedent." Subdivision (b) caps that exposure: "[t]he personal liability of any petitioner shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death of the property received by that petitioner pursuant to an order under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property." Subdivisions (c) and (d), which this clause does not quote verbatim, let the petitioner assert any defense, cross-complaint, or setoff the decedent could have asserted, and bar enforcement of any claim already barred under the estate's creditor-claim statute; subdivision (e) makes Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2 applicable to an action under this section.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(a) Subject to subdivisions (b), (c), and (d), the petitioner who receives the decedent’s property pursuant to an order under this chapter is personally liable for the unsecured debts of the decedent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13156(a), California Probate Code, personal liability for the decedent's unsecured debts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13156.)
  "(b) The personal liability of any petitioner shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent’s death of the property received by that petitioner pursuant to an order under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13156(b), California Probate Code, statutory cap on that personal liability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13156.)

ATTORNEY'S FEES, AND HOW THIS PROCEDURE DIFFERS FROM THE SMALL ESTATE AFFIDAVIT, THE REAL PROPERTY AFFIDAVIT, AND FULL PROBATE
California Probate Code § 13157 provides that attorney's fees for filing a petition and obtaining a court order under this chapter are "determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court," with a court petition available only if the attorney and client later dispute the fee's reasonableness or the meaning of their agreement. Structurally, this procedure sits between this corpus's other small-estate mechanisms: unlike the personal-property small estate affidavit (Probate Code §§ 13100-13106) and the separate real-property small-value affidavit (§ 13200), both of which involve no court hearing, this procedure requires an actual petition, notice, and a hearing that produces a court order under § 13154. And unlike a full petition for probate, which appoints a personal representative and results in ongoing court-supervised administration of the whole estate, this procedure produces only a one-time court determination that specific real property — limited, under current law, to the decedent's primary residence — has passed to the petitioner.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The attorney’s fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 13157, California Probate Code, attorney's fees for this procedure set by private agreement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=13157.)

expectedJSON.body: The dollar ceiling that governs this procedure is not a single fixed number; California Probate Code § 13152(f) writes a four-part schedule directly into the statute's own text. For a decedent who died before April 1, 2022, the applicable amount is $166,250. For a death on or after April 1, 2022 through March 31, 2025, the applicable amount is "the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent's death" — a figure this section does not itself restate. For a death on or after April 1, 2025 through March 31, 2028, the statute states a new flat figure directly: $750,000. For a death on or after April 1, 2028, the applicable amount reverts to whatever adjusted figure is then published under § 890. This entire schedule, including the current $750,000 figure, was written into § 13152 by Stats. 2024, Ch. 331 (AB 2016), effective January 1, 2025.

citations.quote: (f) (1) If the decedent dies prior to April 1, 2022, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is one hundred sixty-six thousand two hundred fifty dollars ($166,250). (2) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2022, through March 31, 2025, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent’s death. (3) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2028, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is seven hundred fifty thousand dollars ($750,000). (4) If the decedent dies on or after April 1, 2028, the dollar amount for paragraph (2) of subdivision (a) is the adjusted dollar amount, published in accordance with subdivision (c) of Section 890, in effect on the date of the decedent’s death.

expectedJSON.body: California Probate Code § 13152(a) requires the petition to be verified by each petitioner and to state, among other things, facts establishing proper venue and that the real property's gross value (as shown by an attached inventory and appraisal) does not exceed the applicable dollar ceiling. Among the petition's other required contents, § 13152(a)(7) requires disclosure of "the name, age, address, and relation to the decedent of each heir and devisee of the decedent," the names and addresses of anyone named as an executor of the decedent's will, and, where the petitioner is trustee of a trust that is itself a devisee under the will, the names and addresses of persons interested in that trust. Separately, § 13152(b) requires an inventory and appraisal, in the form set out in Probate Code § 8802, to be attached to the petition, with the appraisal made by a probate referee the petitioner selects from those the Controller has appointed under § 400 for the county where the property is located.

citations.quote: (a) The petition shall be verified by each petitioner, shall contain a request that the court make an order under this chapter determining that the property described in the petition is property passing to the petitioner, and shall state all of the following: (1) The facts necessary to determine that the petition is filed in the proper county. (2) The gross value of the real property that was the decedent’s primary residence in this state, as shown by the inventory and appraisal attached to the petition, does not exceed the dollar amount specified in subdivision (f).

First, California Probate Code § 13151(b) requires a successor who files this petition to "deliver a notice of the petition to each heir and devisee named in the petition pursuant to paragraph (7) of subdivision (a) of Section 13152" within five business days of filing. expectedJSON.body: California Probate Code § 13154(a) provides that if the court makes the determinations required under subdivision (b), the court "shall issue an order determining that the real property that was the decedent's primary residence...is property passing to the petitioners and the specific property interest of each petitioner in the described property." Subdivision (b)'s required determinations include the property's gross value, the 40-day wait, the applicable no-proceeding-or-consent condition, and that the described property is in fact property of the decedent passing to the petitioner. Section 13154(c) then supplies an evidentiary shortcut on the value determination specifically: where the petition has an inventory and appraisal attached that satisfies § 13152(b), the court makes the gross-value determination "on the basis of the verified petition and the attached inventory and appraisal," unless a person opposing the petition offers evidence that the property's gross value actually exceeds the applicable dollar ceiling.

expectedJSON.body: Receiving property under this chapter carries a liability consequence. California Probate Code § 13156(a) provides that, subject to subdivisions (b) through (d), "the petitioner who receives the decedent's property pursuant to an order under this chapter is personally liable for the unsecured debts of the decedent." Subdivision (b) caps that exposure: "[t]he personal liability of any petitioner shall not exceed the fair market value at the date of the decedent's death of the property received by that petitioner pursuant to an order under this chapter, less the amount of any liens and encumbrances on the property." Subdivisions (c) and (d), which this clause does not quote verbatim, let the petitioner assert any defense, cross-complaint, or setoff the decedent could have asserted, and bar enforcement of any claim already barred under the estate's creditor-claim statute; subdivision (e) makes Code of Civil Procedure § 366.2 applicable to an action under this section.

expectedJSON.body: California Probate Code § 13157 provides that attorney's fees for filing a petition and obtaining a court order under this chapter are "determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court," with a court petition available only if the attorney and client later dispute the fee's reasonableness or the meaning of their agreement. Structurally, this procedure sits between this corpus's other small-estate mechanisms: unlike the personal-property small estate affidavit (Probate Code §§ 13100-13106) and the separate real-property small-value affidavit (§ 13200), both of which involve no court hearing, this procedure requires an actual petition, notice, and a hearing that produces a court order under § 13154. And unlike a full petition for probate, which appoints a personal representative and results in ongoing court-supervised administration of the whole estate, this procedure produces only a one-time court determination that specific real property — limited, under current law, to the decedent's primary residence — has passed to the petitioner.

citations.quote: The attorney’s fees for services performed in connection with the filing of a petition and obtaining a court order under this chapter shall be determined by private agreement between the attorney and the client and are not subject to approval by the court.
